narrative:
The model estimated a 65.9% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means it judged failure to be more likely than not—roughly two chances in three—and that estimate led to the denial of your law school application. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty, and it did not use your gender or race.

The denial was driven mainly by your academic history as summarized in three factors. Your third-year class-rank grouping was the most influential factor and pushed the prediction toward failure; your value was 1.00, compared with about 5.79 among accepted students. Your undergraduate GPA was the second most influential factor and, in this case, pushed toward passing, even though your 2.70 is below the accepted-student average of 3.23. Your first-year class-rank grouping was the third most influential factor and also pushed toward failure; your value was 1.00 versus an accepted-student average of about 6.00. Your LSAT score of 32, below the accepted average of 37.18, adds to the overall concern even though it was not among the top three drivers.

Next, ask admissions whether a human review or appeal is available, and provide any context you believe was missing. To strengthen a future application, focus on raising your LSAT score, demonstrating improved academic performance, and preparing early for bar-exam-style work.
